clue.text: Politician embraces, in professional style, Lydia's aunt

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so the politician's letters wrap round the rest

parts.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament
à la means 'in the style of', the clue's 'style' rounding off the sense
pro is short for a professional

explanation.surface: A politician hugs a relative of someone called Lydia with practised polish.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop, famous for misused words, is the aunt of Lydia Languish in Sheridan's play The Rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's comic character in The Rivals is guardian and aunt to the heroine Lydia Languish.

clue.text: Dreadful putting so many in a tiny environment

indicators.note: an environment surrounds whatever is placed in it, so the tiny phrase wraps round the other letters

parts.note: wee is Scottish and informal for tiny
taken as written
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

explanation.surface: Putting such a crowd into a cramped little space would be dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'environment' puts SOM inside A WEE, splitting WEE after its first E.
explanation.definitionFit: In its older sense the word means inspiring dread or awe, terrifying.

clue.text: Sea-bird winged around every second

indicators.note: the winged word goes around the sea-bird, enclosing it

parts.note: alate is a botanical and zoological term for having wings
a tern is a sea-bird

explanation.surface: A sea-bird flies in circles, wheeling round every second.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking things in turn, one in two, is the adjective's sense of every other one.

clue.text: Tell how a church VIP was beheaded

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter of the church dignitary comes off

parts.note: a prelate is a bishop or other high church official

explanation.surface: Recount the story of how a bishop lost his head.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell a story is to narrate or recount it.

clue.text: Hamlet in sorry state without him

definitions.text: Hamlet in sorry state without him

parts.words: Hamlet in sorry state without him
parts.note: the saying about staging Shakespeare's tragedy without its title character, who is the royal heir

explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is the royal heir of Denmark, and the play without him is the proverbial lacking of its key part.

clue.text: Spotted -many a prize from Paris

parts.note: D, the Roman numeral for five hundred, stands for many
in Greek myth Paris awarded the golden apple to Aphrodite

explanation.surface: Seen: a great many prizes handed out from the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris is not the city but the Trojan prince who judged the goddesses' beauty contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Marked with round patches of colour, as a horse's coat can be.

clue.text: Hurled from last ditch as I face end possibly

indicators.note: possibly says these letters could form something else

explanation.surface: Thrown from a trench as I face my possible end.
explanation.definitionFit: Last-ditch resistance is a bold refusal to submit, flung at the enemy.

clue.text: Its last days coincided with Pliny's

definitions.text: Its last days coincided with Pliny's

parts.words: Its last days coincided with Pliny's
parts.note: Pliny the Elder died in AD 79 during the eruption of Vesuvius that buried a Roman town

explanation.definitionFit: The Roman town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, the eruption that killed Pliny the Elder.

clue.text: Registration trouble with rent — lemon the answer?

indicators.note: trouble means disturb, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: A tenant's sign-up is soured by the rent; is a lemon the solution?
explanation.definitionFit: Signing on for a course or into a membership.

clue.text: Fast, the italian's pulse

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
il is Italian for 'the'

explanation.surface: An Italian keeps a fast and checks his heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' is not a heartbeat but an edible seed of the pea family.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulse is the edible seed of a legume, and this small round one is a classic example.

clue.text: Sneak in late

parts.note: late can mean former, as in 'the late chairman'

explanation.surface: Slip in quietly after the deadline.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneak is someone who tells tales to authority, a grass.

clue.text: Xanthippe the shrew untamed by this method? Such irony!

definitions.text: Xanthippe the shrew untamed by this method? Such irony!

parts.words: Xanthippe the shrew untamed by this method? Such irony!
parts.note: Xanthippe was the famously shrewish wife of the Athenian philosopher whose questioning method and feigned ignorance carry his name

explanation.definitionFit: The philosopher's question-and-answer technique and his pretended ignorance are named after him, yet his wife stayed a notorious scold.

clue.text: Something gelid, say, to heat and cool slowly

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken and the result is what it sounds like

parts.note: a jellied eel, a cold dish, played on gelid sounding like jellied

explanation.surface: Something icy might, they say, be warmed and then left to chill gradually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an eel', the jellied kind being a cold London dish, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Metalworkers and glassmakers toughen material by warming it and letting it cool gradually.

clue.text: Chair-borne battle?

parts.note: a carried chair of the eighteenth century shares its name with a French town where a battle was fought in 1870

explanation.definitionFit: The enclosed carried chair is named after a French town, also the site of a Franco-Prussian War battle.

clue.text: Old theologian, brings many fish to the island

parts.note: a school is a large group of fish
the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: An elderly cleric brings a shoal of fish to the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval scholastic, a teacher of philosophy and divinity in the universities.

clue.text: Piggy holds up another animal

indicators.note: the pig-like word holds the other inside it

parts.note: porcine means relating to or like pigs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pig holds up some other creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodent covered in sharp quills, a creature distinct from a pig.

clue.text: Order to puppet to take over supply of drink

parts.note: Punch is the hook-nosed puppet of Punch and Judy shows
in cricket, to bowl is to deliver an over

explanation.surface: Someone tells a marionette to take charge of the refreshments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch, bowl!' is an order telling the puppet to deliver an over, a set of six balls in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A large vessel from which a mixed drink is ladled out at parties.

clue.text: Keep the principal army at home

parts.note: main means chief or principal
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve
in means at home

explanation.surface: Keep the main body of troops stationed at home.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something is to preserve it or keep it going.

clue.text: Who dreams perhaps nostalgically of returning thus?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Who dreams wistfully of heading back like this?
explanation.definitionFit: Heading towards one's house is the direction of travel when going back.

clue.text: Poor visibility — beginnings of rain and light wind

parts.note: mist reduces visibility

indicators.note: takes the first letters of the next two words

parts.note: L is a common abbreviation for light, on bulbs and learner plates

explanation.surface: A forecast of mist, showers starting and a gentle breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light wind' looks like a breeze, but the definition is just 'wind', the cold north wind of southern France.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong cold north wind that blows down the Rhône valley.

clue.text: Pass one bill in ten after amendment

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
an amended text has been changed, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: a/c, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: Approve a single bill out of ten once it has been revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts AC inside TEN, then 'after amendment' rearranges those five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A legislature passes a bill when it makes it law.

clue.text: Belittle worth of each unorthodox writer

indicators.note: unorthodox means unconventional, so these letters are arranged irregularly

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: Demean the value of every unconventional author.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower the value or reputation of something.

clue.text: Rail system once diverted to Beaconsville

parts.note: BR was British Rail, the former national railway

indicators.note: a diverted line is sent another way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The old railway's trains were rerouted to a town called Beaconsville.
explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh market town gives its name to the Brecon Beacons, hence the coined 'Beaconsville'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh town is the place of the Beacons, its national park mountains.

clue.text: One's thus rejected article by Gaelic bard

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown back, so these words are read backwards

parts.note: one is I, and 's is is
so means thus
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone is turned down in this way by a Scottish poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Scottish poet whose supposed epics James Macpherson published in the 1760s.

clue.text: Gas main

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the sea, and Britain's natural gas comes from beneath one

explanation.definitionFit: British natural gas is piped from fields under this body of water, and main is an old word for the ocean.

clue.text: Appearing in The Good Samaritan — an opera

indicators.note: the answer appears within the run of these words

explanation.surface: A new opera features the parable of the good neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: William Vincent Wallace's 1845 opera is set in Madrid.

clue.text: A bit rough, might one describe Ko-Ko's work?

explanation.surface: A slightly rough executioner's job, the clue jokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Short broken waves describe a moderately rough sea, and an axeman's work is all chopping.

clue.text: Victory was his

parts.note: HMS Victory was the flagship of the admiral killed at Trafalgar in 1805

explanation.definitionFit: The admiral commanded from HMS Victory and won at Trafalgar.

clue.text: Race to get heather for starting a fire
